title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 856–858 (Night 195, continuing nights-194), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 195 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. When the ship overturns, each man looks to himself, and the waves carry Marzawān to the foot of the palace where Qamar al-Zamān lies. It is the day King Shahramān holds court; the king sits with his son’s head in his lap while a servant fans him, for Qamar al-Zamān has neither spoken, eaten nor drunk for two days and has grown thinner than a spindle. The vizier, standing at the window over the sea, sees a man near drowning and asks leave to go down and bring him in, in the hope that God will deliver the prince for the good deed. The king grants it with a threat: if the stranger sees his son and goes out to talk of their secrets, the vizier’s head will fall first, for he caused all that has befallen them. The vizier goes down by the palace’s secret door, pulls Marzawān from the sea by his hair, waits until his breath returns, dresses him in fresh clothes and a servant’s turban, and tells him: I was the cause of your rescue, so do not be the cause of my death and yours — and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-fifth night,
sentences.n: al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَرْكَبَ لَمَّا انْقَلَبَتْ بِجَمِيعِ مَا فِيهَا اشْتَغَلَ كُلُّوَاحِدٍ بِنَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-markaba lammā inqalabat bi-jamīʿi mā fīhā ishtaghala kullu wāḥidin bi-nafsihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-ship, when it-turned-over with-all what (was) in-it, busied-himself each one with-himself.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the ship turned over with everything in her, every man looked only to himself.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the overturned ship where the last night left it. The print again sets السعيدان solid, al-saʿīdu and anna run together; the spacing is kept. al-markaba is set up as the subject of anna, but the sentence never returns to it: after the lammā clause a new subject, kullu wāḥidin, takes over, a loose construction usual in this telling. inqalaba bi-, “to turn over with”: bi- takes in all the ship carried, and markab is feminine, as before. ishtaghala bi-, Form VIII, “to be busy with”: bi- marks what occupies one, here “himself”. كلواحد, kullu wāḥidin, “each one”, is printed as one word.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَرْزَوَانُ فَإِنَّ الْمَوْجَ قَذَفَهُ حَتَّى أَوْصَلَهُ إِلَى تَحْتِ قَصْرِ الْمَلِكِ الَّذِي فِيهِ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā Marzawānu fa-inna al-mawja qadhafahu ḥattā awṣalahu ilā taḥti qaṣri al-maliki alladhī fīhi Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-as-for Marzawān, then-indeed the-waves threw-him until it-brought-him to beneath (the) palace (of) the-king which in-it (is) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: As for Marzawān, the waves tossed him until they brought him to the foot of the king's palace, the one in which Qamar al-Zamān was.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … then”: the fa- is required after ammā. mawj, “waves”, a collective, takes a singular verb. qadhafa, “to throw, cast”. awṣala, Form IV, “to bring (someone) to”. ilā taḥti, “to beneath”, a preposition governing a noun used as a preposition. alladhī refers to the palace, qaṣr.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ بِالْأَمْرِ الْمُقَدَّرِكَانَ هٰذَا الْيَوْمُ الَّذِي يَجْتَمِعُ فِيهِ عَلَى الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ أَهْلُ دَوْلَتِهِ وَأَرْبَابُ مَمْلَكَتِهِ لِلْخِدْمَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna bi-al-amri al-muqaddari kāna hādhā al-yawmu alladhī yajtamiʿu fīhi ʿalā al-maliki Shahramāna ahlu dawlatihi wa-arbābu mamlakatihi li-al-khidmati
sentences.l: And-it-was, by-the-matter the-decreed, was this the-day which gather in-it upon the-king Shahramān (the) people (of) his-state and-(the) lords (of) his-kingdom for-the-service.
sentences.i: And, as fate had decreed, this was the day on which the men of King Shahramān’s state and the lords of his kingdom gathered before him to attend him.
sentences.n: The print sets المقدر and كان solid, al-muqaddari kāna; the spacing is kept. kāna comes twice: the first opens the sentence, “and it was”, and after the phrase bi-al-amri al-muqaddari, “by the decreed matter”, that is, by fate, the second takes it up again, a loose doubling of the spoken style. bi- here is “by, according to”. ijtamaʿa ʿalā, Form VIII, “to gather around, before (someone)”. ahl al-dawla, “the people of the state”, its officers; arbāb, plural of rabb, “lord, master”. li-al-khidma, “for service”: li- of purpose, the formal attendance at court. Shahramāna is genitive with fatḥa, a diptote.

sentences.t: وَالْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ جَالِسٌ وَرَأْسُ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فِي حِجْرِهِ وَخَادِمٌ يَنُشُّ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-maliku Shahramānu jālisun wa-raʾsu waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni fī ḥijrihi wa-khādimun yanushshu ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-the-king Shahramān (was) sitting, and-(the) head (of) his-son Qamar al-Zamān (was) in his-lap, and-a-servant whisking over-him.
sentences.i: King Shahramān was sitting with the head of his son Qamar al-Zamān in his lap, while a servant whisked the flies from him.
sentences.n: Three clauses without a verb, each a picture: wa-al-maliku … jālisun, wa-raʾsu … fī ḥijrihi, wa-khādimun yanushshu. ḥijr, “lap”. nashsha, impf. yanushshu, “to whisk away (flies)”; with ʿalā, over the one being fanned. The shadda of ينشّ and the hamza of رأس are printed, and here the print writes fī with ي, في.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مَضَى لَهُ يَوْمَانِ مَا تَكَلَّمَ وَلَا أَكَلَ وَلَاشَرِبَ وَصَارَ أَنْحَفَ مِنَ الْمِغْزَلِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna Qamaru al-Zamāni maḍā lahu yawmāni mā takallama wa-lā akala wa-lā shariba wa-ṣāra anḥafa mina al-mighzali
sentences.l: And-was Qamar al-Zamān (that) passed for-him two-days not he-spoke and-not ate and-not drank, and-he-became thinner than the-spindle.
sentences.i: Two days had passed for Qamar al-Zamān in which he had neither spoken nor eaten nor drunk, and he had grown thinner than a spindle.
sentences.n: kāna takes a whole clause as its predicate: “Qamar al-Zamān was (such that) two days had passed for him”. yawmāni, dual, “two days”. mā with the perfect denies the past, and wa-lā carries the denial on; the print runs lā into its verb, ولاشرب, and the spacing is kept. anḥafa min, elative, “thinner than”, accusative as the predicate of ṣāra. mighzal, “spindle”, a byword for thinness. The shadda of تكلّم is printed.

sentences.t: وَالْوَزِيرُ وَاقِفٌ عِنْدَ رِجْلَيْهِ قَرِيبَ الشُّبَّاكِ الْمُطِلِّ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-wazīru wāqifun ʿinda rijlayhi qarība al-shubbāki al-muṭilli ʿalā al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-the-vizier (was) standing at his-two-feet, near the-window the-overlooking onto the-sea.
sentences.i: The vizier stood at his feet, near the window that looked out over the sea.
sentences.n: rijlayhi, “his two feet”, dual. qarība, “near”, an accusative used as a preposition. shubbāk, a latticed window. muṭill ʿalā, active participle of Form IV aṭalla, “overlooking”. The shadda of المطلّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَرَفَعَ الْوَزِيرُ بَصَرَهُ فَرَأَى مَرْزَوَانَ قَدْ أَشْرَفَ عَلَى الْهَلَاكِ مِنَ التَّيَّارِ وَبَقِيَ عَلَى آخِرِ نَفَسٍ
sentences.tr: fa-rafaʿa al-wazīru baṣarahu fa-raʾā Marzawāna qad ashrafa ʿalā al-halāki mina al-tayyāri wa-baqiya ʿalā ākhiri nafasin
sentences.l: And-raised the-vizier his-sight, and-saw Marzawān: already he-had-come-near onto the-perishing from the-current, and-remained on (the) last (of a) breath.
sentences.i: The vizier raised his eyes and saw Marzawān, brought by the current to the edge of death and down to his last breath.
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to look down upon”, hence “to be on the brink of”; qad with the perfect, “had already”. halāk, “perishing”. min, “from”, gives the cause: the tayyār, “current”. ʿalā ākhiri nafasin, “at the last of a breath”. The hamza of فرأى, the shadda of التيّار and the madda of آخر are printed.

sentences.t: فَرَقَّ عَلَيْهِ قَلْبُ الْوَزِيرِ فَتَقَرَّبَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ وَمَدَّ رَأْسَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-raqqa ʿalayhi qalbu al-wazīri fa-taqarraba ilā al-maliki wa-madda raʾsahu ilayhi wa-qāla lahu
sentences.l: And-grew-tender over-him (the) heart (of) the-vizier, and-he-drew-near to the-king and-stretched his-head to-him and-said to-him:
sentences.i: The vizier’s heart was moved for him; he drew near to the king, leaned his head toward him and said,
sentences.n: raqqa ʿalā, “to grow tender toward, pity”, with the heart as subject. taqarraba ilā, Form V, “to draw near to”. madda raʾsahu, “he stretched out his head”, leaning in to speak low. The shaddas of فرقّ and مدّ and the hamza of رأسه are printed.

sentences.t: أَسْتَأْذِنُكَ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ فِي أَنْ أَنْزِلَ إِلَى سَاحَةِ الْقَصْرِ وَأَفْتَحَ بَابَهَا لِأَ نْقُلَ إِنْسَانًا قَدْ أَشْرَفَ عَلَى الْغَرَقِ فِى الْبَحْرِ وَأُطْلِعَهُ مِنَ الضِّيقِ إِلَى الْفَرَجِ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ بِسَبَبِ ذٰلِكَ يُخَلِّصُ وَلَدَكَ مِمَّا هُوَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: astaʾdhinuka ayyuhā al-maliku fī an anzila ilā sāḥati al-qaṣri wa-aftaḥa bābahā li-anqula insānan qad ashrafa ʿalā al-gharaqi fī al-baḥri wa-uṭliʿahu mina al-ḍīqi ilā al-faraji laʿalla Allāha bi-sababi dhālika yukhalliṣu waladaka mimmā huwa fīhi
sentences.l: I-ask-your-leave, O king, in that I-go-down to (the) courtyard (of) the-palace and-open its-gate, so-that-I-may-carry a-human who has-come-near onto the-drowning in the-sea, and-bring-him-up from the-narrowness to the-relief; perhaps God by-cause (of) that will-free your-son from-what he (is) in-it.
sentences.i: “O king, I ask your leave to go down to the courtyard of the palace and open its gate, so that I may bring in a man who is on the point of drowning in the sea, and lift him out of distress into relief; it may be that for this God will free your son from the state he is in.”
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, corrected here. istaʾdhana fī, Form X, “to ask leave for”: fī marks the thing asked. The print sets the next verb as two words, لا نقل; it is read here as one, li-anqula, li- “so that” with the subjunctive of naqala, “to carry, convey”, the hamza of the verb’s a- written on the alif of the first piece, and the spacing is kept. This is a guess at a doubtful place: one letter away, لانقذ, li-anqidha, “so that I may rescue”, would suit as well, but it is not what the print has. aṭlaʿa, Form IV, “to bring up”, in the subjunctive after li- like anqula. ḍīq and faraj, “straits” and “relief”, are a set pair. laʿalla Allāha … yukhalliṣu: this time no an after laʿalla. bi-sababi, “by reason of”: bi- of cause. The hamza and sukūn of استأْذنك and the shadda of لعلّ are printed; the print writes fī as فى in this unit.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ يَكْفِي مَاجَرَى عَلَى وَلَدِي مِنْكَ وَبِسَبَبِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku ayyuhā al-wazīru yakfī mā jarā ʿalā waladī minka wa-bi-sababika
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-king: O vizier, (it) suffices what happened upon my-son from-you and-by-your-cause.
sentences.i: The king said to him, “Vizier, enough has befallen my son through you and because of you.
sentences.n: yakfī, “it is enough”, used almost as an interjection, as in the spoken language: “enough of what has happened …”. jarā ʿalā, “to befall”: ʿalā marks the one it falls on. The print runs mā into its verb, ماجرى. minka wa-bi-sababika, “from you and by your cause”: bi- of cause. The king blames the vizier, whose counsel to press the youth to marry began the trouble.

sentences.t: وَرُبَّمَا أَنَّكَ إِذَا أَطْلَعْتَ هٰذَا الْغَرِيقَ يَطَّلَّعُ عَلَى أَحْوَالِنَا وَيَنْظُرُ إِلَى وَلَدِي وَهُوَ فِى هٰذِهِ الْحَالَةِ فَيَشْمَتُ بِي
sentences.tr: wa-rubbamā annaka idhā aṭlaʿta hādhā al-gharīqa yaṭṭallaʿu ʿalā aḥwālinā wa-yanẓuru ilā waladī wa-huwa fī hādhihi al-ḥālati fa-yashmatu bī
sentences.l: And-perhaps that-you, if you-brought-up this the-drowning-man, he-will-pry into our-affairs and-look at my-son while-he (is) in this the-state, and-gloat over-me.
sentences.i: And it may well be that, if you bring this drowning man up, he will pry into our affairs and look on my son in this state, and gloat over me.
sentences.n: rubbamā annaka …, “perhaps that you …”: rubbamā, “perhaps”, takes anna here, a Middle Arabic turn, and the sentence then changes subject: after the idhā clause the drowning man, not “you”, is the one who pries. يطلّع, with its printed shadda on the lām, is read yaṭṭallaʿu, Form V taṭallaʿa with its t merged into the ṭ, “to look into, pry into”, with ʿalā of what is looked into. gharīq, “one drowned, drowning”. shamita bi-, “to rejoice at the misfortune of”: bi- marks the one gloated over. wa-huwa …, “while he (is)”, a circumstantial clause.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أُقْسِمُ بِاللَّهِ إِنْ طَلَعَ هٰذَا الْغَرِيقُ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى وَلَدِي وَخَرَجَ يَتَحَدَّثُ مَعَ أَحَدٍ بِأَسْرَارِنَا لَأَضْرِبَنَّ رَقَبَتَكَ قَبْلَهُ لِأَنَّكَ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ سَبَبُ مَاجَرَى لَنَا أَوَّلًا وَآخِرًا
sentences.tr: wa-lākin uqsimu bi-Allāhi in ṭalaʿa hādhā al-gharīqu wa-naẓara ilā waladī wa-kharaja yataḥaddathu maʿa aḥadin bi-asrārinā la-aḍribanna raqabataka qablahu li-annaka ayyuhā al-wazīru sababu mā jarā lanā awwalan wa-ākhiran
sentences.l: But I-swear by-God: if comes-up this the-drowning-man and-looks at my-son and-goes-out talking with anyone of-our-secrets, I-will-surely-strike your-neck before-him, because-you, O vizier, (are the) cause (of) what happened to-us, first and-last.
sentences.i: But I swear by God, if this drowning man comes up and sees my son, and goes out and talks of our secrets to anyone, I will strike off your head before him; for you, vizier, are the cause of all that has befallen us, first and last.
sentences.n: uqsimu bi-Allāhi, “I swear by God”: bi- of the oath. in with the perfect, “if (he) …”, of the future. taḥaddatha bi-, Form V, “to talk of”: bi- marks what is told. la-aḍribanna, the oath’s la- with the energetic -anna, “I will surely strike”; ḍaraba raqabatahu, “to strike someone’s neck”, to behead. qablahu, “before him”: the vizier dies first, then the man. li-anna, “because”. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks those it befalls. awwalan wa-ākhiran, “first and last”. The shaddas of يتحدّث, لاضربنّ, ايّها and اوّلا and the madda of وآخرا are printed.

sentences.t: فَافْعَلْ مَا بَدَالَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ifʿal mā badā laka
sentences.l: So-do what seemed-good to-you.
sentences.i: So do as you see fit.”
sentences.n: badā li-, “to seem good to”: li- marks the one to whom it seems so. The print runs badā and laka together, ما بدالك; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ الْوَزِيرُ وَفَتَحَ بَابَ سِرِّ الْقَصْرِ النَّافِذَ إِلَى الْبَحْرِ وَنَزَلَ فِى الْمَمْشَاةِ عِشْرِينَ خُطْوَةً ثُمَّ خَرَجَ إِلَى الْبَحْرِ فَرَأَى مَرْزَوَانَ مُشْرِفًا عَلَى الْمَوْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa al-wazīru wa-fataḥa bāba sirri al-qaṣri al-nāfidha ilā al-baḥri wa-nazala fī al-mamshāti ʿishrīna khuṭwatan thumma kharaja ilā al-baḥri fa-raʾā Marzawāna mushrifan ʿalā al-mawti
sentences.l: And-rose the-vizier and-opened (the) door (of the) secret (of) the-palace, the-leading-through to the-sea, and-went-down in the-walkway twenty steps, then went-out to the-sea, and-saw Marzawān nearing onto the-death.
sentences.i: The vizier rose and opened the palace’s secret door that led through to the sea; he went down the passage twenty paces, then came out at the sea, and saw Marzawān at the point of death.
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, corrected here. bāb sirr, “a door of secrecy”, a private postern; al-nāfidha, “leading through”, agrees with bāb. al-mamshāti: the print spells mamshā, “walk, passage”, with a final ة, a spelling of the time; kept. ʿishrīna khuṭwatan, “twenty paces”: after ʿishrūn the counted noun is a singular accusative. mushrifan, accusative of state: “nearing death”.

sentences.t: فَمَدَّ الْوَزِيرُ يَدَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَمَسَكَهُ مِنْ شَعْرِ رَأْسِهِ وَجَذَبَهُ مِنْهُ فَخَرَجَ مِنَ الْبَحْرِ وَهُوَ فِى حَالِ الْعَدَمِ وَقَدِ امْتَلأَ بَطْنُهُ مَاءً وَبَرَزَتْ عَيْنَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-madda al-wazīru yadahu ilayhi wa-masakahu min shaʿri raʾsihi wa-jadhabahu minhu fa-kharaja mina al-baḥri wa-huwa fī ḥāli al-ʿadami wa-qadi imtalaʾa baṭnuhu māʾan wa-barazat ʿaynāhu
sentences.l: And-stretched the-vizier his-hand to-him and-took-hold-of-him by (the) hair (of) his-head and-pulled-him by-it, and-he-came-out from the-sea, and-he (was) in (the) state (of) the-nothingness, and-already had-filled his-belly (as to) water, and-bulged-out his-two-eyes.
sentences.i: The vizier stretched out his hand to him, caught him by the hair of his head and drew him out by it; he came out of the sea all but lifeless, his belly filled with water and his eyes bulging.
sentences.n: masaka, “to take hold of”, the spoken form where Classical prose has amsaka, Form IV. min, “by”, marks the part held, and minhu, “by it”, the hair he was pulled by. fī ḥāli al-ʿadami, “in the state of nothingness”, as good as dead. imtalaʾa, Form VIII, “to be filled”, with māʾan, “water”, an accusative saying with what. barazat ʿaynāhu, “his two eyes stood out”. The shadda of فمدّ and the hamzas of رأسه and امتلأ are printed.

sentences.t: فَصَبَرَ الْوَزِيرُ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّى رُدَّتْ رُوحُهُ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣabara al-wazīru ʿalayhi ḥattā ruddat rūḥuhu ilayhi
sentences.l: And-waited-patiently the-vizier over-him until was-returned his-spirit to-him.
sentences.i: The vizier waited patiently over him until his life was given back to him.
sentences.n: ṣabara ʿalā, “to bear patiently with, wait on”. ruddat, passive of radda, “to give back”; rūḥ, “spirit, life”, is feminine. In the spoken language radda can also stand alone for “to come back”, so raddat rūḥuhu, “his spirit came back”, is possible too. The shadda of ردّت is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَعَ عَنْهُ ثِيَابَهُ وَأَلْبَسَهُ ثِيَابًا غَيْرَهَا وَعَمَّمَهُ بِعِمَامَةٍ مِنْ عَمَائِمِ غِلْمَانِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma nazaʿa ʿanhu thiyābahu wa-albasahu thiyāban ghayrahā wa-ʿammamahu bi-ʿimāmatin min ʿamāʾimi ghilmānihi
sentences.l: Then he-stripped from-him his-clothes and-clothed-him (in) clothes other-than-them, and-turbaned-him with-a-turban of (the) turbans (of) his-pages.
sentences.i: Then he stripped him of his clothes, dressed him in others, and put on him a turban from among his pages’ turbans.
sentences.n: nazaʿa ʿan, “to pull off from”. albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the clothes. ʿammama, Form II, “to put a turban on (someone)”: bi- marks the turban. ghilmān, plural of ghulām, “page, young servant”. The shadda of عمّمه and the ئ of عمائم are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي كُنْتُ سَبَبًا لِنَجَاتِكَ مِنَ الْغَرَقِ فَلَا تَكُنْ أَنْتَ سَبَبًا لِمَوْتِي وَمَوْتِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu iʿlam annī kuntu sababan li-najātika mina al-gharaqi fa-lā takun anta sababan li-mawtī wa-mawtika
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Know that-I was a-cause for-your-rescue from the-drowning, so-not be you a-cause for-my-death and-your-death.
sentences.i: And he said to him, “Know that I was the cause of your rescue from drowning; so see that you are not the cause of my death and yours.”
sentences.n: sababan li-, “a cause of”: li- marks what is caused. lā takun, lā of prohibition with the jussive, “do not be”; anta, “you”, is stressed. The vizier has the king’s oath in mind: if Marzawān talks, the vizier’s head is forfeit, and the stranger’s life with it. The sentence runs over the night’s end without a break.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. Here the print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept.
